title: UIViewController Lifecycle & View Hierarchy
summary: The concrete UIKit view-controller callback sequence and containment model — what belongs in each method, and the two mistakes that cause broken layouts and retain cycles.

slides.markdown:
Every screen in a UIKit app is a `UIViewController`, and every one of them goes through the same predictable sequence of callbacks from creation to disappearance. Put the wrong work in the wrong callback and you get symptoms that look unrelated to the real cause: a layout that's off by a few pixels, a table view that flickers on push, a screen that leaks every time it's dismissed.

This topic is the exact ordering, what UIKit guarantees at each step, and the containment model — navigation controllers, tab bars, and child view controllers — that most real screens are built from rather than one controller alone.

For a screen being pushed and later dismissed, UIKit calls, in this exact order:

1. `loadView` — creates the root view (you almost never override this).
2. `viewDidLoad` — fires **once**, after the view hierarchy is loaded into memory.
3. `viewWillAppear` — every time the screen is about to become visible.
4. `viewWillLayoutSubviews` / `viewDidLayoutSubviews` — around Auto Layout passes.
5. `viewDidAppear` — the screen is now fully on screen and interactive.
6. `viewWillDisappear` / `viewDidDisappear` — the mirror image on the way out.

The critical fact hiding in that list: `viewDidLoad` runs once per controller instance, but `viewWillAppear`/`viewDidAppear` run **every single time** the screen becomes visible — including returning from a pushed detail screen.

Two timelines run alongside each other and it's easy to conflate them: the **controller lifecycle** (the callbacks above) and the **view hierarchy's own loading** (views getting created, added as subviews, then measured and positioned by Auto Layout).

`viewDidLoad` fires after the hierarchy exists in memory but **before** it has real frames — every view's `bounds` is still whatever Interface Builder or your init code set, not the actual on-screen size. Frames only become trustworthy inside or after `viewWillLayoutSubviews`.

slides.subTitle: what belongs in each
slides.markdown:
The single most common lifecycle question, because the two are easy to mix up:

| | viewDidLoad | viewWillAppear |
|---|---|---|
| Fires | once per instance | every time the screen becomes visible |
| Frames reliable? | no | closer, but layout may still adjust |
| Put here | one-time setup: subview creation, static config, delegates | data that can go stale: refresh a list, re-check a toggle |
| Wrong to put here | data that changes between visits | expensive one-time work (runs repeatedly) |

A classic bug: fetching a list only in `viewDidLoad` means a user who edits an item on a detail screen and pops back sees stale data, because the fetch never re-runs. Move the refresh to `viewWillAppear` and it's correct on every return visit, not just the first.

slides.subTitle: navigation, tab bar, and child VCs
slides.markdown:
Most real screens aren't one lone view controller — they're composed through **containment**. A `UINavigationController` manages a stack of view controllers and pushes/pops between them; a `UITabBarController` swaps between several root controllers; and you can build your own containment by adding a **child view controller** whose view is embedded inside a parent's.

Containment changes lifecycle timing: a child added via `addChild(_:)` gets its own `viewDidLoad`/`viewWillAppear` calls, but the parent is responsible for forwarding appearance transitions correctly if it manages appearance manually (`shouldAutomaticallyForwardAppearanceMethods`). Get this wrong and a child's `viewWillAppear` either double-fires or never fires when the parent's does.

A very common bug: reading a view's `bounds` or `frame` inside `viewDidLoad` to do manual layout math (sizing a gradient layer, calculating a corner radius relative to width) and getting `0` or a stale value back.

The cause is the ordering from the diagram above — `viewDidLoad` runs before Auto Layout has resolved real frames. The fix is to move that work to `viewWillLayoutSubviews` or `viewDidLayoutSubviews`, which fire specifically **after** the layout engine has settled frames, and can fire multiple times (rotation, keyboard, size class change) — so guard against redoing expensive work every call, not just moving it there once.

Containment is built on **strong** references both ways by design: a parent holds strong references to its children (`UIViewController.children`), and it's easy to accidentally add a strong reference back — a child holding a strong `parent: MyParentVC` property instead of using the built-in weak `self.parent`, or a delegate property on the child that isn't declared `weak`.

The symptom is a screen that never deallocates after being popped or dismissed — `deinit` simply never runs, memory grows on every push/pop cycle, and Instruments' memory graph shows the parent and child keeping each other alive. The fix: use UIKit's built-in `parent`/`children` accessors instead of your own strong properties, and mark any custom delegate or callback property on a child `weak`.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: appearance transitions aren't guaranteed pairs
slides.markdown:
A subtlety that trips up mid-level engineers: `viewWillAppear` and `viewDidAppear` are not perfectly guaranteed to always pair 1:1 with `viewWillDisappear`/`viewDidDisappear` in every interruption scenario — a fast, interrupted transition (the user yanks back a swipe-to-pop gesture partway) can leave you needing to check `isMovingToParent`/`isBeingDismissed`/`transitionCoordinator` to know *why* an appearance callback fired, not just *that* it fired.

The practical takeaway for interviews: don't just recite the six method names. Say what each one guarantees and doesn't — `viewDidLoad` guarantees hierarchy existence, not real frames; `viewWillAppear` guarantees an impending appearance, not that the transition will complete uninterrupted. That distinction is what separates reciting the lifecycle from actually being able to debug it.

SwiftUI's declarative model replaces most of this with view identity and `.onAppear` — covered in its own topic, [SwiftUI Fundamentals](swiftui-fundamentals).
